claim: The image reconstruction framework is based on Bayesian image reconstruction from the excitations of the retinal cone mosaic.
source: We developed an image-computable observer model of the initial visual encoding that operates on natural image input, based on the framework of Bayesian image reconstruction from the excitations of the retinal cone mosaic.
evidence: The abstract directly states the methodological basis of the framework.

claim: The model extends previous work on ideal observer analysis and evaluation of performance beyond psychophysical discrimination.
source: Our model extends previous work on ideal observer analysis and evaluation of performance beyond psychophysical discrimination, takes into account the statistical regularities of the visual environment, and provides a unifying framework for answering a wide range of questions regarding the visual front end.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a contribution of the work.

claim: The model takes into account the statistical regularities of the visual environment.
source: Our model extends previous work on ideal observer analysis and evaluation of performance beyond psychophysical discrimination, takes into account the statistical regularities of the visual environment, and provides a unifying framework for answering a wide range of questions regarding the visual front end.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this feature of the model.

claim: Large variations in the assignment of L and M cones (nearly a 10-fold range) have little impact on the average reconstruction error.
source: Interestingly, we found that large variations (nearly a 10-fold range) in the assignment of L and M cones have little impact on the average reconstruction error (Figure 4A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 4A which shows the data.

claim: The average reconstruction error as a function of the proportion of S cones shows a clear optimum at a small S-cone proportion (~10%).
source: On the other hand, the average reconstruction error as a function of the proportion of S cones shows a clear optimum at a small S-cone proportion (~10%; Figure 4B).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 4B which shows the data.

claim: The empirically observed allocation of retinal photoreceptor type is consistent with the principle of optimal design.
source: Our results are in agreement with a previous analysis in showing that the empirically observed allocation of retinal photoreceptor type is consistent with the principle of optimal design (Garrigan et al., 2010; also see Levin et al., 2008; Manning and Brainard, 2009; Sampat et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2017).
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion and cites supporting literature.

claim: The indifference to L/M ratio can be explained by the large spatial and chromatic correlations present in natural images, together with the high overlap in L- and M-cone spectral sensitivities.
source: The indifference to L/M ratio can be explained by the large spatial and chromatic correlations present in natural images, together with the high overlap in L- and M-cone spectral sensitivities.
evidence: The text explicitly provides this explanation for the observed result.

claim: The sensitivity to S cone proportion is due to a combination of chromatic aberrations and the fact that S cones mainly contribute to the estimation of pixel values in the B-pixel plane.
source: Additional analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) revealed that the sensitivity to S cone proportion is due to a combination of two main factors: (1) chromatic aberrations, which blur the retinal image at short wavelengths and reduce the value of dense spatial sampling at these wavelengths; and (2) S cones mainly contribute to the estimation of pixel values in the B-pixel plane, whereas L and M cone contribute to both the R- and G-pixel planes (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this explanation and references supporting figure.

claim: The dependence of the average reconstruction error on the L-cone proportion decreases as the chromatic correlation in the signal increases.
source: The dependence of the average reconstruction error on the L-cone proportion decreases as the chromatic correlation in the signal increases (Figure 5).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 5 which shows the data.

claim: A decrease of spatial correlation has little impact on the shape of the curves, but increases the overall magnitude of reconstruction error.
source: A decrease of spatial correlation has little impact on the shape of the curves, but increases the overall magnitude of reconstruction error (Figure 5; to highlight the shape, the scale of the y-axis is different across rows and columns. See Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for the same plot with matched y-axis scale).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding and references Figure 5.

claim: Natural images are thought to have both high spatial and high chromatic correlation.
source: Natural images are thought to have both high spatial and high chromatic correlation (Webster and Mollon, 1997; Nascimento et al., 2002; Garrigan et al., 2010), making the results shown in Figure 5 consistent with those in Figure 4.
evidence: The text explicitly states this property of natural images and cites supporting literature.

claim: Each type of dichromacy creates a distinct pattern of color confusions and shifts in the reconstructed color.
source: While the spatial structure of the original images is largely retained in the reconstructions, each type of dichromacy creates a distinct pattern of color confusions and shifts in the reconstructed color.
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation about dichromatic reconstructions.

claim: The difference between the original images and each of the corresponding dichromatic reconstructions is driven by the image prior.
source: Note that in the case where there is no simulated cone noise (as in Figure 6), the original image has a likelihood at least as high as the reconstruction obtained via our method. Thus, the difference between the original images and each of the corresponding dichromatic reconstructions is driven by the image prior.
evidence: The text explicitly states this explanation for the observed differences.

claim: At high light intensities, the reconstructions are similar for the normal and deuteranomalous mosaics.
source: At high light intensities, the reconstructions are similar for the normal and deuteranomalous mosaics (first row).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation about reconstructions at high light intensities.

claim: At lower intensities, the deuteranomalous reconstruction lacks chromatic content still present in the normal reconstruction.
source: At lower intensities, however, the deuteranomalous reconstruction lacks chromatic content still present in the normal reconstruction (second and third row).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation about reconstructions at lower light intensities.

claim: A loss of chromatic content is also seen for the reconstruction from the normal mosaic at the lowest light level.
source: Furthermore, a loss of chromatic content is also seen for the reconstruction from the normal mosaic at the lowest light level (last row).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation about normal mosaic reconstructions at low light.

claim: Biological visual systems that operate at low light levels are typically monochromatic, potentially to increase the SNR of spatial vision at the cost of completely disregarding color.
source: This observation may be connected to the fact that biological visual systems that operate at low light levels are typically monochromatic, potentially to increase the SNR of spatial vision at the cost of completely disregarding color (e.g. the monochromatic human rod system; see Manning and Brainard, 2009 for a related and more detailed treatment; also see Walls, 1942; Rushton, 1962; van Hateren, 1993; Land and Osorio, 2003).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation about biological visual systems and cites supporting literature.

claim: The degradation in the quality of the reconstructed images can be clearly observed as we move from the fovea to the periphery.

claim: For some retinal locations, the elongated point-spread function (PSF) also introduces a salient directional blur.
source: For some retinal locations, the elongated point-spread function (PSF) also introduces a salient directional blur (Figure 8E and F).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation and references specific panels in Figure 8.

claim: There is a trade-off across visual eccentricity between spatial and chromatic vision.
source: Concretely, in Figure 8, we observe a trade-off across visual eccentricity between spatial and chromatic vision.
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation about the reconstructions.

claim: In the image of the dragonfly, the reconstructed colors are desaturated at intermediate eccentricities compared with the fovea and more eccentric locations.
source: In the image of the dragonfly, for example, the reconstructed colors are desaturated at intermediate eccentricities (e.g. Figure 8C and D), compared with the fovea (Figure 8A) and more eccentric locations (Figure 8E and F).
evidence: The text explicitly describes this observation and references specific panels in Figure 8.

claim: A larger PSF does lead to better estimate of chromatic content, albeit eventually at the cost of spatial content.
source: This revealed that (Figure 8—figure supplement 3): (1) A larger PSF does lead to better estimate of chromatic content, albeit eventually at the cost of spatial content.

claim: An appropriate amount of optical blur is required to achieve the best overall image reconstruction performance, presumably due to its prevention of aliasing.
source: (2) In general, an appropriate amount of optical blur is required to achieve the best overall image reconstruction performance, presumably due to its prevention of aliasing.

claim: The optical cut-off of the eye is reasonably matched to the spacing of the photoreceptors (i.e. the mosaic Nyquist frequency), enabling good spatial resolution while minimizing spatial aliasing due to discrete sampling.
source: Both in humans and other species, it has been noted that the optical cut-off of the eye is reasonably matched to the spacing of the photoreceptors (i.e. the mosaic Nyquist frequency), enabling good spatial resolution while minimizing spatial aliasing due to discrete sampling (Williams, 1985; Snyder et al., 1986; Land and Nilsson, 2012).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation and cites supporting literature.

claim: With instruments that bypass the physiological optics and present high contrast grating stimuli directly on the retina, human subjects can detect spatial frequencies up to 200 cyc/deg.
source: Experimentally, it has been demonstrated that with instruments that bypass the physiological optics and present high contrast grating stimuli directly on the retina, human subjects can detect spatial frequencies up to 200 cyc/deg (Williams, 1985).
evidence: The text explicitly states this experimental finding and cites the source.

claim: For foveal viewing, subjects report having a percept resembling a pattern of 'two-dimensional noise' and/or 'zebra stripes' when viewing high spatial frequency stimuli.
source: For foveal viewing, subjects also report having a percept resembling a pattern of 'two-dimensional noise' and/or 'zebra stripes' when viewing those high spatial frequency stimuli (Williams, 1985).
evidence: The text explicitly states this experimental finding and cites the source.

claim: For peripheral viewing, high frequency vertical gratings can be perceived as horizontal (and vice-versa).
source: For peripheral viewing, high frequency vertical gratings can be perceived as horizontal (and vice-versa; Coletta and Williams, 1987).
evidence: The text explicitly states this experimental finding and cites the source.

claim: The reconstructions recapitulate the 'zebra stripe' percept reported at approximately 120 cyc/deg in the fovea.
source: Concretely, the reconstructions recapitulate the 'zebra stripe' percept reported at approximately 120 cyc/deg in the fovea (Figure 9A); as well as the orientation-reversal effect at an appropriate spatial frequency in the periphery (Figure 9B).

claim: The reconstructions recapitulate the orientation-reversal effect at an appropriate spatial frequency in the periphery.

claim: For achromatic grating stimuli viewed under diffraction-limited conditions, additional chromatic aliasing should be visible.
source: Since our method accounts for trichromacy, we have also made the prediction that for achromatic grating stimuli viewed under similar diffraction-limited conditions, while the spatial aliasing pattern will be comparable, additional chromatic aliasing should be visible (Figure 9—figure supplement 2; also see Williams et al., 1991; Brainard, 2015).
evidence: The text explicitly states this prediction and references the supporting figure.

claim: The image-reconstruction based observer shows significant interactions between spatial frequency and chromatic direction.
source: The image-reconstruction observer shows significant interactions between spatial frequency and chromatic direction.

claim: Sensitivity in the L + M direction is relatively constant with spatial frequency.
source: Sensitivity in the L + M direction is relatively constant with spatial frequency.

source: Sensitivity in the L – M direction starts out higher than L + M at low spatial frequencies, but drops significantly and is lower than L + M at high spatial frequencies (Figure 10B).

source: It is intriguing that the CSFs from the reconstruction-based observer show substantially higher sensitivity for L - M than for L + M modulations at low spatial frequencies (with equated RMS cone contrast), but with a more rapid falloff such that the sensitivity for L + M modulations is higher at high spatial frequencies.

claim: The forward model is implemented within the open-source software package ISETBio.
source: Our forward model is implemented within the open-source software package ISETBio (isetbio.org; Figure 1A–C) which encapsulates the probabilistic relationship between the stimulus (i.e. pixel values of a displayed RGB image) and the cone excitations (i.e. trial-by-trial photopigment isomerizations).

source: ISETBio simulates the process of displaying an image on a monitor (Figure 1A), the wavelength-dependent optical blur of the human eye and spectral transmission through the lens and the macular pigment (Figure 1B), as well as the interleaved spatial and chromatic sampling of the retinal image by the L, M, and S cones (Figure 1C).
